Predict Landscape Scales for New Covariates and Groups

Source: R/bayes_scale_predict_scales.R
predict_scales.Rd

Carry joint posterior uncertainty into the scale of each landscape predictor at new values of the scale-formula covariates, including years that were not surveyed when the scale formula has a random year effect. This predicts the scale itself, so no prepared landscape is needed.

Usage

predict_scales(
  object,
  newdata,
  new_levels = c("error", "sample", "zero"),
  re.form = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  draws = NULL,
  summary = TRUE,
  scale = c("distance", "log"),
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

object

A fitted multiScale_bayes() object with stored joint posterior draws, from sampling or either approximation.

newdata

A nonempty data frame that holds the fixed scale-formula covariates and the grouping variables of any included scale random effects. Responses, response-only covariates, and prepared landscape bins are not needed.

new_levels

What to do with a scale group level that was not in the fitted data. "error" (default) stops and asks for a decision. "sample" draws a new standardized group effect for each joint posterior vector. "zero" sets the new deviation to zero. Known levels keep their fitted effects. Neither choice creates a coefficient for an unseen level of a fixed factor.

re.form

NULL (default) includes the scale random effects. NA sets every scale deviation to zero, a reference value rather than an average over group variation. Response effects are never used here.

level

Probability of the central interval; default 0.95.

draws

Optional positive integer number of evenly spaced stored posterior vectors to use. The default NULL uses every vector.

summary

Logical. TRUE (default) returns interval summaries and computes each repeated scale combination once, which avoids a large matrix when many rows share one year's scale. FALSE returns one matrix of draws by new observations for each landscape predictor.

scale

"distance" (default) returns projected map units. "log" returns natural log distances in those units.

seed

Optional positive integer seed for sampled new effects. Your own random-number state is restored afterward, even when prediction fails.

Value

With summary = TRUE, a data frame with one row per landscape predictor and distinct active combination of scale covariates and groups.

  • covariate: the landscape predictor.

  • group: a label for the covariates and groups of the row, such as "year=2026".

  • row: a representative row of newdata.

  • new_level: whether the row contains an unseen scale group.

  • distribution: which question the row answers. See "Read the distribution column".

  • mean, median, sd, lower, upper: summaries of the draws on the requested scale, with the central level interval. Prefer the median and the limits for distances. See posterior_scales() for why the arithmetic mean and SD of a distance can be poorly defined.

  • p_below_min_D, p_above_max_D: the probability that the scale lies below min_D or above max_D of the fitted inputs. See "Read the support columns".

With summary = FALSE, a named list with one numeric matrix per landscape predictor. Each matrix has one row per posterior vector and one column per row of newdata, in the supplied order. Rows in the same new group share its effect.

Both forms carry a new_groups attribute with component, covariate, group, level, and action, listing the unseen levels that were sampled or set to zero. Summaries also carry a prediction_contract attribute (see prediction_contract) that describes the target, the included scale effects, and the uncertainty. It does not establish diagnostic eligibility or calibration.

Read the distribution column

  • "conditional_posterior": a surveyed group, using its estimated deviation.

  • "new_group_predictive": the range of scales a new group could have. Its interval carries uncertainty in the typical scale and in the between-group SD, plus the variation among groups. It is a marginal prediction interval, not a simultaneous band and not an estimate of a new year's scale after its responses are observed.

  • "zero_deviation_reference": the new group placed exactly at the typical scale (with new_levels = "zero"), or every group with re.form = NA. Its interval keeps uncertainty in the typical scale but leaves out variation among groups, so it is narrower without being a more precise forecast.

The zero-deviation reference is not the average scale over years. With \(\log D_y = a + \tau z_y\), even for fixed a and tau the mean of \(D_y\) over years is \(\exp(a + \tau^2/2)\), while the zero-deviation scale is \(\exp(a)\). Averaging over the uncertainty in a and tau also depends on their posterior dependence.

Read the support columns

p_below_min_D and p_above_max_D refer to the range of the fitted inputs. They say nothing about the coverage of a future map you have not supplied. The distance priors have no upper or lower bound, so these probabilities matter when much of the posterior lies outside the distances your maps resolve. A scale below min_D is finer than one raster cell.

To check a future map, compare the scale draws with that map's max_D. The scale parameter is not the reach of the kernel. Under an ideal, untruncated planar kernel, the radius that holds 95% of the weight is kernel_dist(prob = 0.95, sigma = 1, kernel = fit$specification$kernel) times the scale. The examples compute both probabilities. Neither measures actual cell coverage near raster edges or gaps, which you should inspect separately. A smaller future buffer renormalizes a more truncated kernel. If larger neighborhoods are scientifically needed, rebuild comparable fitting and prediction inputs and refit, rather than changing the predictor's support only at prediction time.

Predict new groups jointly

A new year's sampled effect is shared by all of that year's rows within one posterior vector. Different new years are independent given the population parameters, whose posterior dependence is kept. Effects for separate model components follow their specified independence. Separate calls draw separate new effects, so put rows that belong together in one batch. Exchangeable annual effects impose no temporal autocorrelation. A fitted numeric trend extrapolates under that trend assumption, and an unseen level of a fixed year factor is an error.

Know the limits

The method uses the stored joint draws, which for an importance-corrected fit are stored resamples. It adds no posterior information and does not validate a failed fit. A nonfinite distance stops with an error, so use scale = "log" for extreme scales. Fitted contrasts and prediction-aware bases such as scale(), poly(), and the splines keep their training constants, including inside nested expressions such as I(scale(temp)). Fits saved by older versions need verified recovery from the original training data. An expression such as I(x - mean(x)) takes its mean from the new batch by ordinary R formula rules, so use a prediction-aware basis or precomputed training constants when the original centering matters. Formula transforms must come from base R or stats, or carry an explicit package namespace.

See also

posterior_scales(), prediction_contract, predict.multiScaleR_bayes(), simulate.multiScaleR_bayes(), kernel_dist(), multiScaleR_bayes; vignette("v14-bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR").

Examples

example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-prediction-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
fit <- example$fit   # habitat scale varies among years 2021 to 2025
years <- data.frame(year = c("2025", "2026"))   # 2026 was not surveyed

# A surveyed year, then a new year drawn from the spread among years
predict_scales(fit, years, new_levels = "sample", draws = 500,
  seed = 801)[c("group", "distribution", "median", "lower", "upper")]
#>       group          distribution   median    lower    upper
#> 1 year=2025 conditional_posterior 152.7981 43.31996 375.6791
#> 2 year=2026  new_group_predictive 161.1544 37.54491 513.8587
# The reference: the new year placed at the typical scale
predict_scales(fit, years[2, , drop = FALSE], new_levels = "zero",
  draws = 500)[c("group", "distribution", "median", "lower", "upper")]
#>       group             distribution   median    lower    upper
#> 1 year=2026 zero_deviation_reference 157.4092 49.96857 408.1584

# Can a future map of the same extent hold the new year's kernel?
log_D <- predict_scales(fit, years[2, , drop = FALSE], new_levels = "sample",
  scale = "log", summary = FALSE, draws = 500, seed = 806)$habitat
max_D <- example$kernel_inputs$max_D   # 1200 m for the future inputs
radius_per_D <- kernel_dist(prob = 0.95, sigma = 1,
  kernel = fit$specification$kernel)
mean(log_D > log(max_D))                       # scale itself beyond max_D
#> [1] 0.002
mean(log_D + log(radius_per_D) > log(max_D))   # 95% radius beyond max_D
#> [1] 0.03
# The second probability is larger, because the kernel reaches past its
# scale parameter.
